beats.say: This looks complex, but a name, a year and an exclamation mark are the first pattern attackers try.
Better: a passphrase of four or more random words. Long, easy to remember and very hard to guess.

visual.label: Just an example, make your own

beats.say: Length beats complexity. Aim for at least fifteen characters; spaces or hyphens between words are fine.

options.label: Pa$$w0rd2026
options.feedback: Letter swaps are well known to cracking tools.

options.label: camel lantern lemon cloud
options.feedback: Right. Four random words are long and unpredictable.

beats.say: When one site leaks, attackers try that password on other sites. So every account needs its own.

scenes.prompt: Create a passphrase of your own.
tips: Do not type your real password here, this is practice.
Pick four or more random words.
Avoid song lyrics, poems and proverbs.
Leave out names, dates and your workplace.

scenes.prompt: Find the signs of a fake in this leak alert.

subject.text: Your password was found in a leak

body.text: Your password was found in a leaked database online.
enter your old and new password in this form.
If you do not act within one hour, the account will be deleted.

spots.label: Fake domain
spots.explain: The agency's domain is xidmetagentliyi.az, with no -az.com at the end.

spots.label: Generic greeting
spots.explain: Your own security team would write to you by name.

spots.label: Asks for old password
spots.explain: A real service does not ask you to type your old password into a form from an email. Change it yourself on the site you know.

spots.label: Foreign link
spots.explain: The link goes to another domain, not the agency's site.

spots.label: One-hour threat
spots.explain: A short deadline and a threat push you to act without thinking.

scenes.title: Reset your password
scenes.intro: After a leak warning, a password reset page opens in the browser. Read the address and decide.

steps.label: Your password was found in a leak
steps.say: The page scares you and rushes you. Whose address is it?

actions.label: Reset password here
actions.feedback: After a leak warning, do not follow the link. Change the password on a site you open yourself.

actions.label: Close tab, I will open the portal myself
actions.feedback: Right: hesab-yoxla.info is not the agency's site. Open the portal yourself from a bookmark.

steps.say: The form wants your old password too. Check the address.

actions.label: Reset password
actions.feedback: A fake form that asks for the old password steals it. Change it on the official portal now and report it.

actions.label: Close tab
actions.feedback: Right. parol-yenile.info is not the agency's domain, so type nothing here.

actions.label: Report site
actions.feedback: Great. Reporting the fake site helps get it blocked for others too.

steps.label: You opened the portal yourself
steps.say: This is the agency's own portal. What do you do now?

actions.label: Change password
actions.feedback: Right, you changed it on the official portal. Make the new one a long phrase used nowhere else.

actions.label: I will change it later
actions.feedback: If the password leaked, someone may already be trying it. Change it on the official portal now.

options.label: Length matters more than complexity
options.feedback: Right. A long password is far harder to crack.

options.label: A separate password for every account
options.feedback: Right. Then one leak puts only one account at risk.

options.label: Change your password every month
options.feedback: Changing without a reason often leads to weak, similar passwords. Change it at once if you suspect a leak.

options.label: A birth year helps you remember
options.feedback: A birth year is easy to find, and attackers try it first.

scenes.explain: Current advice: long, unique passwords, changed at once after a leak. If your organisation's rules differ, follow them.

points: A long passphrase beats a short complex password.
A separate password for every account.
After a leak, change the password at once.
